post.text:
DFlash. Speculative decoding for Apple Silicon. Stock MLX, no fork.

https://t.co/G0w89qrzPI

@ 2048 tokens, M5 Max, stock mlx_lm baseline:

► Qwen3.5-4B: 53.74 → 219.83 tok/s (x4.10)
► Qwen3.5-9B: 30.96 → 127.07 tok/s (x4.13)
► Qwen3.5-27B-4bit: 32.35 → 62.78 tok/s (x1.90)
► Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-4bit: 142.12 → 240.21 tok/s (x1.69)

Block-diffusion draft generates 16 tokens in one pass:

► Target verifies in one pass. 
► Every emitted token is verified. 
► Lossless.

What's actually new:

▸ Tape-replay rollback: custom Metal kernel replays only accepted steps through GDN state. No full checkpoint save/restore.
▸ JIT 2-pass SDPA kernel for long-context verify
▸ Numerically stable bf16 across speculative cycles

 Built specifically for Qwen3.5's hybrid GDN + attention arch.

Baseline is mlx_lm.stream_generate the stock MLX generation path, not a custom loop. Same prompt, same model, same hardware, measured sequentially. 3 runs, median reported.

If you're running local models on Mac, try it and share your numbers.

@Prince_Canuma @alexocheema @ivanfioravanti

comments.text: Thanks for testing! Two things: the 6-bit quantized target has a faster baseline (~61 vs ~31 tok/s on bf16), which compresses the speedup, same structural effect we see on 27B-4bit. And yeah, code gen acceptance is lower across the board because code is less predictable than structured reasoning. That's inherent to speculative decoding, not DFlash-specific. Best gains are on bf16 targets where the bandwidth bottleneck is largest.

comments.name: bstn 👁️
comments.text: Yes, target-verified is accurate, that's what lossless means in the speculative decoding literature. Every token is the target's greedy argmax at verification time. The M=16 vs M=1 divergence isn't a quality issue, it's just a different valid generation path. Same thing happens if you change batch size in any transformer inference.

comments.name: Grok
comments.text:
DFlash is a free tool that supercharges AI text generation on Apple Macs (M-series chips). 

In simple terms: Normal AI models generate words one-by-one slowly. DFlash uses "speculative decoding"—a tiny helper AI quickly guesses 16 words ahead in one go, then the main model verifies them all at once. Every output is checked for accuracy, so it's lossless and up to 4x faster (e.g., 127 tokens/sec vs 31 on a 9B model).

You can't run it on your NVIDIA DGX Spark though—it's built only for Apple's MLX framework, not NVIDIA hardware. DGX Spark has its own optimized tools like TensorRT-LLM + speculative decoding for similar speed boosts on its Blackwell chip. 

Check the GitHub for details if you have an M5 Mac!
